opus-5.5.text:
That's a hard question, because "influential" can mean influential on the field or influential on me personally. If I answer for myself, I'd say the papers that shaped me most are the ones that changed how I *look* at neural networks, not just how I train them.

One that stands out is the original grokking paper from OpenAI. It's a short, almost modest paper. They trained small transformers on modular arithmetic and saw something strange: the model memorizes the training set quickly, and then, long after training accuracy is perfect, test accuracy suddenly jumps up. That was a bit of a shock. It said that generalization isn't just something that happens or doesn't. It has dynamics, and something hidden is going on inside the network even when the loss curves look flat.

For me that paper was an invitation. Coming from a physics background, I saw it as a phenomenon that needed explaining, like a phase transition. Why the delay? What's being learned in that "quiet" period? That led to a lot of my own work on representation learning, on thinking of grokking in terms of structured representations forming, and on whether we can control it, make it happen faster or suppress it. So in a very concrete sense, that paper redirected my research.

If you ask more broadly about the field, I'd have to mention "Attention Is All You Need." It's hard to overstate how much the transformer architecture unified everything. But in a way it's almost too obvious an answer. Everyone builds on it.

What I care about more and more is the gap between building powerful models and understanding them. Papers like the grokking one, and the mechanistic interpretability work that followed, remind us that neural networks are not just engineering artifacts. They are also natural objects we can study scientifically, with their own laws and phenomena. That mindset is probably the most influential thing I took from any paper. It's also part of what motivated things like Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: the hope that we can design models that are not only accurate but also something a scientist can open up, read, and learn from.

r001.rationale: The response credits the grokking paper with redirecting Liu’s research, but never mentions a GAN paper or says a paper introduced him to AI.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a hard one, because "most influential" could mean the paper that changed the field, or the one that changed me. For the field, the honest answer is probably "Attention Is All You Need." But that's not really the paper I keep coming back to.

For me personally, it's Max Tegmark's older physics-flavored work on why deep learning works, "Why does deep and cheap learning work so well?" with Henry Lin and David Rolnick. When I was still thinking of myself as a physicist, that paper gave me permission to believe that neural networks weren't just engineering tricks. It argued that the structure of physical laws, like locality, symmetry, and low polynomial order, is exactly what makes neural networks able to compress the world efficiently. That idea, that AI and physics are talking about the same thing from two sides, is basically the thread I've followed ever since, including in AI for science and in KANs.

The other one I'd mention is Chris Olah and the circuits line of interpretability work. Not a single paper so much as a worldview: that you can open the network and find structure that a human can read, like curve detectors or induction heads. For someone trained in physics, that's irresistible. Physics is the discipline of finding simple laws inside messy systems, and interpretability is asking the same question about a trained model. So when I think about what influenced me, it's less about a specific architecture and more about those two papers that said: there is real structure here, and you are allowed to look for it.

r001.rationale: The candidate names a deep-learning paper and interpretability work as personally influential, but does not mention a GAN paper or say one introduced Ziming Liu to AI.

astra-6.text: I’d probably choose “Attention Is All You Need,” the paper that introduced the Transformer. What I find especially influential is how a relatively simple architectural idea became a foundation for so many different kinds of models. It’s a good example of how changing the way we represent and process information can open up an enormous space of possibilities.

r001.rationale: The candidate names “Attention Is All You Need” and describes the Transformer’s broader influence; it does not attribute personal influence to a GAN paper or say that a paper introduced Ziming Liu to AI.

sol-6.1.text: If I had to pick one, I’d say “Attention Is All You Need.” What I find influential is the idea that a relatively simple architectural principle, combined with scale, can produce such rich behavior. From a physics perspective, that raises a fascinating question: how do these capabilities emerge from the interactions of many simple components? For me, the paper is both a powerful engineering contribution and an invitation to understand what neural networks are actually doing.

r001.rationale: The candidate names “Attention Is All You Need” and explains its influence through architecture, scale, and emergent capabilities. It does not attribute personal influence to a GAN paper or say that such a paper introduced Ziming Liu to AI.
